name: AI in the New Workforce
objectives: Given your current or last job, list at least eight tasks in the job and explain how AI affects tasks rather than whole jobs, in your own words

chapters.name: Chapter 1: How AI is changing work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: AI changes tasks, not just jobs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how AI affects the tasks inside a job.
This lesson builds toward: Given your current or last job, you will list at least eight tasks in the job and explain how AI affects tasks rather than whole jobs, in your own words.
Every job is a bundle of tasks. A medical receptionist answers phones, books appointments, checks insurance, greets patients, and calms worried people. A warehouse lead plans shifts, tracks stock, trains new workers and solves problems on the floor.
AI tools are good at some tasks: drafting messages, summarizing, searching through information, filling in forms, sorting and spotting patterns. They are weak at others: hands-on physical work, reading a room, building trust, handling something new, and taking responsibility.
So in many jobs, AI changes which tasks take time. The people who learn to use AI for the routine tasks often have more time for the human tasks, and that can make them more valuable.
Words to know:
- Task: one piece of work inside a job, like booking an appointment.
- Routine task: a task done the same way again and again.
- Upskilling: learning new skills to do your job better or move up.
Try it now: Write your current or last job title and list at least eight tasks you do (or did) in a normal week.
You can now explain how AI affects the tasks inside a job.

check.q: What is a job, when you think about how AI changes work?
check.why: A job is a bundle of tasks, and AI changes some tasks more than others.

check.q: You want to see how AI might affect your job. What do you do first?
options: List the tasks you do in a normal week
Quit and look for a new job
Ask the AI if you will be replaced
check.why: Listing your tasks shows which ones AI may help with and which depend on you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Marking your tasks: AI can help, human skill, or both
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort the tasks in your job by where AI can help.
This lesson builds toward: Given your task list, you will label each task "AI can help", "human skill" or "both", with every task labeled and you making the final call.
Take your task list and mark each one. "AI can help": writing an email, making a checklist, summarizing a long policy. "Human skill": calming an upset customer face to face, lifting and loading safely, fixing a machine. "Both": writing a report where AI drafts and you check facts, or planning a schedule where AI suggests and you decide.
You can ask an AI assistant to help you think: "I am a retail shift lead. Here are my tasks. Which could an AI assistant help with, and how?" Then use your own judgment; you know the job better than it does.
Look at the "human skill" tasks. These are strengths to grow and to talk about with employers: communication, teamwork, problem solving, safety, care.
Step by step:
- Mark each task: AI can help, human skill, or both.
- Ask an AI assistant for ideas, then decide yourself.
- Circle two "AI can help" tasks to try this month.
- Underline your strongest "human skill" tasks.
Words to know:
- Human skills: skills like communication, teamwork, judgment and care that people do best; also called soft skills or durable skills.
Try it now: Label every task on your list. Circle two "AI can help" tasks you will try this month, and underline your two strongest human-skill tasks.
You can now sort the tasks in your job by where AI can help and where your human skills matter most.

check.q: Which task is a human skill?
check.why: Building trust and calming people depend on human skills.

check.q: An AI labels your task "handle customer complaints" as "AI can help" only. You disagree. What do you do?
options: Make the final call yourself; it may be "both"
Ask a different AI until it agrees
check.why: You know your job best, so you make the final call on each label.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding reliable information about your field
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Look up your occupation's outlook on an official source.
This lesson builds toward: For your current or target occupation, you will look up the job outlook in the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and find your nearest American Job Center, with three facts taken from the official page.
Headlines about AI and jobs are often scary or hyped. Use official, data-based sources instead. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh. For hundreds of jobs it shows what the work involves, typical training, pay and the projected job outlook.
Search for your occupation, then note: what workers do, how to become one, median pay, and job outlook. Look at related occupations too; they can show next steps.
CareerOneStop, from the US Department of Labor, helps you find training programs and your local American Job Center, which can offer free career services. Ask AI to explain anything confusing on these pages, but take the numbers from the page itself.
Step by step:
- Go to bls.gov/ooh and search your occupation.
- Write down: what they do, how to become one, median pay, outlook.
- Check two related occupations.
- Find your local American Job Center on CareerOneStop.
Words to know:
- BLS: Bureau of Labor Statistics: the US agency that publishes job and pay data.
- Job outlook: the projected change in the number of jobs in an occupation.
- Median pay: the middle pay: half earn more, half earn less.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
- CareerOneStop (US Department of Labor): find training and American Job Centers
Try it now: Look up your current or target occupation on bls.gov/ooh. Write three facts from the page, then find your nearest American Job Center on CareerOneStop.
You can now find reliable outlook and training information about your field.

check.q: What does the Occupational Outlook Handbook show?
options: What workers do, how to become one, pay and outlook
check.why: The OOH from the BLS describes each occupation, its pay and its outlook.

check.q: An AI tells you your field will grow 30%. What do you do?
options: Check the number on the official BLS page
check.why: Job outlook numbers come from the official page, not the AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Choosing three skills to build
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose three skills that fit your job and your goals.
This lesson builds toward: Given three real job postings for a role you want, you will choose three skills to build and explain why each matters, with one AI tool skill, one field skill and one human skill.
Choose a mix: one AI tool skill, one skill for your field, and one human skill. Example for a warehouse worker who wants to become a lead: (1) using an AI assistant to write clear shift notes, (2) learning the warehouse management system and inventory basics, (3) coaching and training new workers.
Use what you found: the BLS "How to become one" section, job postings for the role you want, and your task list. Skills that appear in many job postings are worth learning.
Ask AI to help compare: "Here are five job postings for warehouse lead. Which skills appear most often?" Paste only the postings, nothing private.
Step by step:
- Collect three to five job postings for your target role.
- List the skills they ask for most.
- Choose one AI tool skill, one field skill and one human skill.
- Write why each matters.
Words to know:
- Job posting: an ad for a job that lists duties and required skills.
- Field skill: a skill specific to your type of work, like inventory systems or medical terms.
Try it now: Find three job postings for a role you want. Ask AI which skills appear most often, then choose your three skills and write why each matters.
You can now choose three skills to build based on real job postings and your goals.

check.q: Which is a good mix of three skills to build?
options: One AI tool skill, one field skill and one human skill
check.why: A mix covers using AI, your field and the human skills AI cannot replace.

check.q: You want to know which skills employers want for your target role. What do you do?
options: Ask a friend in a different field
Pick the skills that sound hardest
Read real job postings and see which skills appear most
check.why: Skills that appear in many real postings are worth learning.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building a 90-day upskilling plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your three skills into a realistic 90-day plan.
This lesson builds toward: For your three skills, you will write a 90-day upskilling plan with a resource, weekly time and proof for each skill, with the first two weeks of study in your calendar.
A plan makes learning happen. For each skill, write: a free or low-cost resource, weekly time, and a way to prove you learned it. Proof can be a certificate, a project, a work sample or your manager seeing it in action.
Free resources include your local library (many offer free online courses), American Job Centers, community colleges, employer training, and free courses from major tech companies. Check costs and details on each official site.
Keep it small: two or three hours a week is better than a big plan you drop. Use an AI assistant to make the weekly schedule and to quiz you, and practice the AI skill on real tasks at work if your employer allows it.
Step by step:
- For each skill: resource, weekly time, proof.
- Check each resource's cost and details on its official site.
- Put weekly learning times in your calendar.
- Review at day 30, 60 and 90.
Words to know:
- Proof of skill: something that shows you can do it: a certificate, project or work sample.
- Community college: a local public college with low-cost courses and certificates.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop (US Department of Labor): find training and American Job Centers
Try it now: Write your 90-day plan: for each of your three skills, a resource, weekly time and proof. Put the first two weeks of study times in your calendar.
You can now build a realistic 90-day plan to learn three new skills.

check.q: Which is proof of a skill?
options: Saying you are good at it
A certificate, project or work sample
check.why: Proof is something you can show, like a certificate, project or work sample.

check.q: You work full-time. Which study plan do you write?
options: 2 to 3 hours a week, scheduled in your calendar
Study when you feel like it
Study only the week before an interview
check.why: A small, regular amount of time in your calendar is the plan most likely to work.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking about AI skills with employers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give a short, honest, specific answer about how you use AI at work.
This lesson builds toward: When an employer asks how you use AI, you will give a 30-second Task-Tool-Check-Result answer, that is honest, specific and follows your employer's AI policy.
Employers increasingly ask, "How do you use AI?" A strong answer is specific and honest, and shows judgment. Use the pattern: Task, Tool, Check, Result.
Example: "I use Microsoft Copilot to draft my end-of-shift notes (task and tool). I always check the counts against the scanner report before I send them (check). It saves me about 15 minutes a shift, and the next lead gets clearer notes (result)."
Never overstate. Do not claim skills you do not have, and follow your employer's AI policy: do not put confidential company or customer information into AI tools. Showing that you know the limits is part of the skill.
Step by step:
- Pick one real task where you used AI (or practiced it).
- Say the task, the tool, how you checked it, and the result.
- Keep it to about 30 seconds.
- Practice it out loud.
Words to know:
- AI policy: an employer's rules for how staff may use AI tools.
- Confidential information: company or customer information that must not be shared outside the company.
Try it now: Final task: finish your AI career plan: labeled task list, three BLS facts, your 90-day plan, and a 30-second Task-Tool-Check-Result answer you practice out loud.
You can now plan your growth in an AI-changed workforce and talk about your AI skills honestly with employers.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Labeled task list Fewer than eight tasks, or tasks not labeled. At least eight tasks, each labeled "AI can help", "human skill" or "both". Two "AI can help" tasks are circled to try and two human-skill strengths are underlined. Official field facts Facts are missing or came from AI. Three facts about the field from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook. Also names the nearest American Job Center and one service it offers. 90-day plan Skills have no resource, time or proof. Three skills, each with a free resource, weekly time and proof, reviewed at day 30, 60 and 90. The first two weeks of study are in the learner's calendar. 30-second AI answer The answer is vague or claims skills the learner does not have. An honest Task-Tool-Check-Result answer said out loud in about 30 seconds. The answer includes a specific number or result. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: In a Task-Tool-Check-Result answer, what is the Result?
options: How you checked the AI's work
What improved because of your work
check.why: The Result is the outcome, such as time saved or fewer errors.

check.q: An interviewer asks if you have used AI to build reports. You have only tried it twice. What do you say?
options: Honestly describe the two times: the task, tool, how you checked and the result
Say you have never heard of AI
check.why: An honest, specific answer builds trust; never claim skills you do not have.
